catalog_quote: Rutooro (E/J.12), a Ugandan Bantu language, is one of only a handful of Bantu languages in which tone is no longer lexically contrastive. Although Rutooro does not have contrastive tone, all words in isolation are pronounced with a prominence on the penultimate syllable, which we refer to as High (H) tone. [...] The distribution of H tones is nontrivial in phrasal contexts, where it is neither the case that each word has a H on the penultimate syllable, nor that every utterance is restricted to a single H on the final penult. [...] When larger sentences are examined, it is possible to find nearly any combination of toneless words and H-marked words, but the utterance-final penult will always be marked with a H tone. [...] In accounting for the distribution of high tones in Rutooro, we first establish that H tones link to the penultimate syllable of each phonological phrase (ϕ-phrase), as illustrated in (4). (4) High tone insertion σ σ)ϕ ∅ → H

new_statements.rule_in_words: Rutooro has lost lexical tone; prominence (realized as a High pitch) falls predictably on the penultimate syllable. Every word in isolation/citation form has penult prominence; in connected speech the H is assigned to the penult of each phonological phrase (right edge of syntactic XPs), so phrase-medial words can surface all-Low while the utterance-final penult is always H. Independently confirmed by Kaji 2010 (ZASPiL 53: 99, 103): 'the penultimate syllable of the word is always high-pitched in isolation' / 'All nouns are pronounced with high tone on the penultimate syllable in isolation', and Bickmore 2019 fn.: 'a High is predictably found on the penult of each phonological phrase.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; non-phrase-final words are described as all-Low (no secondary prominence mentioned).
new_statements.exceptions: Prominence placement itself has no lexical exceptions; what varies is which words receive it: nouns before weak determiners/adjectives/reduced relatives, verbs followed by arguments, and nouns followed by possessive -ange (Kaji 2010) surface without H because they are not phi-phrase-final; Kaji notes tone still has grammatical (phrasal) functions, e.g. ekitabu kyaange 'my book' vs Ekitabu kyaange 'the book is mine'. Clemens & Bickmore fn. 11: a head noun may bear H before a modifier with a monosyllabic root.
new_statements.domain_note: Authors treat the prominence as a predictable H tone whose assignment domain is the phonological phrase, not the word; citation forms (words in isolation) always show penult prominence. An alternative coding would be 'phrase-level prominence only'; 'fixed: penultimate syllable' is chosen because position within the domain is invariantly penultimate and isolation forms are penult-prominent. Language is described as toneless (no lexical tone), so this is not a tone-language case.
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted sources describe Rutooro/Tooro proper (toor1238, Fort Portal area; Clemens & Bickmore's consultant is from Fort Portal). Kaji 2010 explicitly contrasts Tooro (lexical tone lost, penult H in isolation) with closely related Nyoro (nyor1246), which retains a two-pattern tonal contrast, so the statement should NOT be extended to 'Runyoro-Rutooro' as a unit; Rubongoya 1999 treats Runyoro-Rutooro jointly.

sources.note: Rutooro lacks lexical/contrastive tone; all words in isolation have prominence (H tone) on the penultimate syllable; in sentences H links to the penult of each phonological phrase (rule (4) High tone insertion: sigma sigma)phi, 0 -> H); utterance-final penult always H; words not at a phi-phrase right edge surface all-Low.

sources.note: p.99: 'Tooro has completely lost its original lexical tone distinction, where the penultimate syllable of the word is always high-pitched in isolation'; p.103 sec.4: 'Tooro has lost its lexical tone. All nouns are pronounced with high tone on the penultimate syllable in isolation (.sss)'; H in isolation disappears when noun is followed by possessive -ange; footnote: tone still fulfills grammatical functions (Kaji 2009).
